summary: RFC 8342 defines the NMDA configuration datastores, whose contents are controlled by clients. This Standards Track document adds a system configuration datastore holding configuration controlled by the system itself. Client configuration can reference it. It updates RFC 8342.

eli5.summary: A device has settings you set and settings it picks itself. This keeps the second kind in its own place you can still look at.

questions: what is the system configuration datastore
how does system datastore merge with running
subtitle: A read-only datastore that exposes configuration the device creates for itself, so clients can see and build on it.

tldr.problem: The NMDA treats system configuration as something the device supplies, visible in the operational datastore only when in use. Operators want a standard way to see what is available, and to reference, override or extend it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 10016 adds a read-only conventional datastore called system. Configuration in running is merged with system to form intended, and running takes precedence on any node it sets.
tldr.outcome: Clients can reference system nodes, override their values and configure their descendants. The RFC updates RFC 8342 and is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Client writes
facts.value: Denied directly; overrides go via running

today: RFC 10016 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2026 that updates RFC 8342. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC.

sections.title: Why a System Datastore
sections.content:
The Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) in RFC 8342 defines system configuration as configuration supplied by the device itself, which appears in <operational> when in use. Operators want servers to expose it whether or not it is in use. Some implementations require system configuration to be referenced before it becomes active, and NETCONF and RESTCONF clients would benefit from a standard way to retrieve what is available.

Some servers also let clients configure descendants of system-defined nodes. For example, a nearly empty physical interface may exist because hardware is present, while the client adds or changes nodes below it. Some nodes, such as the interface type, may not be modifiable.

RFC 10016 updates RFC 8342 with a read-only conventional datastore called system. It requires NMDA for clients and servers, and NMDA servers must implement the ietf-system-datastore YANG module.
sections.eli5: Some of a device's settings are decided by the device, like a built-in light that is always there. Before, it was hard to see them until they were in use. Now there is a place to look.

sections.title: Kinds of System Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC defines two kinds. Always-present configuration is generated in <system> when the device powers on, whether or not physical resources exist. An always-existing loopback interface is the example.

Conditionally present configuration appears when conditions are met. When an interface card is inserted, the system detects it and loads its configuration, and when the card is removed, the configuration is removed from <system>. Enabling a license or feature can also create configuration.

The RFC also defines a referenced node: a leafref target, an instance-identifier target, a node in a when or must XPath expression, or a node needed to satisfy mandatory true or min-elements. System configuration that a server allows to be deleted is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Some built-in things are always there, like a doorbell. Others show up only when you plug something in, and vanish when you unplug it.

sections.title: The System Datastore and the Model
sections.content:
The new datastore is named system, covers all YANG modules, and holds all config true nodes generated by the system. It can be read over NETCONF and RESTCONF but cannot be changed through them. It does not persist across reboots. NMDA servers MUST implement it and SHOULD also implement <intended>. No new origin identity is defined: the existing system origin identity marks data from <system>.

In the updated architecture, <running> is merged with <system> to become <intended>, and <running> takes precedence on the same node. Transformations such as template expansion or removal of inactive configuration MUST be performed on each datastore independently before the merge. Whenever <system> changes, the server MUST immediately update and validate <intended>.

The RFC also redefines conventional configuration datastore to be <running>, <startup>, <candidate>, <system> and <intended>.
sections.eli5: Picture the device's own notes and your notes on two sheets. The device lays your sheet over its sheet and reads the result. Where both say something, yours wins.

sections.title: Referencing, Overriding and Extending
sections.content:
Clients write into <running>, never into <system>; edits aimed directly at <system> MUST be denied. There are three things a client can do with system nodes.

  • Reference: configuration in <running> can point at system nodes, for example through a leafref.
  • Override: if the server allows it, a value in <running> replaces the system value. Some implementations mark immutable nodes with an immutable metadata annotation.
  • Add descendants: a server may let clients add nodes to a list entry in <system>.

Items in <system> cannot be deleted by clients. If an overriding node is removed from <running>, the system-initialized value appears in <intended> again. If configuration disappears from <system> because resources are gone, client configuration for it can stay in <running> and <intended> but is not applied. Changes to <system> may be learned through YANG notifications, and <running> SHOULD remain valid.
sections.eli5: You can point at the device's built-in things, change some of their settings with your own note, or add extra notes underneath. You cannot erase what the device wrote.

sections.title: The ietf-system-datastore Module
sections.content:
The YANG module defines one new identity, system, whose base is ds:conventional from RFC 8342. Clients discover support by reading the YANG library from the operational datastore. The module has revision 2026-09-16 and prefix sysds.

In NETCONF the datastore is read with get-data and the datastore name sysds:system. In RESTCONF it is the resource {+restconf}/ds/ietf-system-datastore:system.

The RFC clarifies origin reporting. Configuration in <system> that is not also in <running> is reported with origin system in <operational>. The intended origin now means configuration explicitly provided by clients. Nothing else about <operational> changes, and config false nodes are out of scope.
sections.eli5: The module is just a new name tag, system, added to the list of shelves. Everything else is how the shelves already work.

sections.title: Security and Operations
sections.content:
The YANG module defines only an identity, so it exposes no sensitive data nodes. The management protocols have to use a secure transport and mutual authentication, and NACM can restrict access.

The system datastore may hold sensitive information such as hardware identifiers and security policies. Read access to sensitive nodes MUST be controlled, and logging access attempts is strongly advised. Because system values can be overridden through <running>, an attacker could configure a leaf that shadows a sensitive system node, so unauthorized modification MUST be prevented.

Operationally, system configuration exists whether or not a server implements <system>. Clients that do not know about it keep working using the other datastores, but must be updated to use <system>.
sections.eli5: The device's own settings can be private, so only the right people may look. And since your notes can cover the device's notes, only trusted people should be allowed to write them.

viz.caption: WHAT A CLIENT CAN DO WITH SYSTEM CONFIGURATION

items.title: Reference
items.text: Point at system nodes from running, for example with a leafref.

items.title: Override
items.text: Set a value in running that takes precedence, if the server allows it.

items.title: Extend
items.text: Add descendant nodes below a system-defined list entry.

items.title: Not allowed
items.text: Edit or delete anything in system directly.
